claims.text: Pre-applying an Al2O3 coating to boride-based components will improve their resistance to corrosion by molten aluminum.
The applied Al2O3 coating should be thin, dense, and adherent.
The pre-applied alumina layer will serve as a stable diffusion barrier between molten aluminum and the boride substrate.
The alumina coating will prevent or slow interdiffusion between molten aluminum and the boride substrate.
The alumina coating will prevent or slow chemical reaction between molten aluminum and the boride substrate.
The alumina barrier will reduce the active contact area between molten aluminum and the boride substrate.
Reducing interdiffusion, reaction, and active contact area will lower the corrosion rate.
Alumina-coated boride components will have a significantly lower corrosion rate than uncoated components under identical molten-aluminum exposure conditions.
Alumina-coated boride components will exhibit lower mass loss than uncoated components after molten-aluminum exposure.
Alumina-coated boride components will exhibit less microstructural degradation than uncoated components after molten-aluminum exposure.
The intervention should remain effective under operating temperatures and molten-aluminum compositions typical of hot-dip plating if the coating remains intact and adherent.
Cracking, delamination, or degradation under cyclic thermal or mechanical stress will reduce the coating's effectiveness.
The stability and long-term adhesion of Al2O3 during prolonged high-temperature molten-aluminum exposure are uncertain.
Failure to obtain a statistically significant reduction in corrosion rate relative to an uncoated control would falsify the hypothesis.
Rapid cracking, delamination, or degradation of the alumina coating under the test conditions would falsify the hypothesis.
